item.content:encoded:
Tonga's 3x3 basketball women team pulled off one of the biggest shocks of the tournament by defeating the host nation, Scotland 12-10, in front of a home crowd, led by sisters Mele and Leslia Finau. Also recording pool stage wins against Papua New Guinea, they went on to defeat Singapore 14-10, earning a spot in the play-in quarter final at the Glasgow 2026 Commonwealth Games this week.

Tonga finished in 3rd place in Pool B, at the SEC Centre, narrowly missing out on an automatic semi-final spot but advancing further into the knockout rounds.

However, last night's clash with Uganda has knocked Tonga out of a place in the semi-finals. This knockout matchup featured Tonga (3rd in Pool B) against Uganda (2nd in Pool A). Uganda relied on an aggressive, commanding inside game with a 21-12 victory advanced Uganda to the semifinals against England.

Leading the successful campaign was the Finau sisters, Lesila and Mele Finau with the pair reflecting on the emotional significance of competing together for the first time since high school.

" It's more than just a match,” Mele Finau said.

She told reporters that the opportunity to represent Tonga at the Commonwealth Games alongside her sister carried special meaning following the death of their father.

" We haven't played together since high school, so I'm about to get emotional," she said.

" It's so amazing, especially since our dad passed.

" This is the main reason why we are doing this - representing him and representing the country."

The 3x3 format features teams of three players competing on a half-court with a single basket. Games last a maximum of 10 minutes, with the first team to reach 21 points declared the winner. Shots inside the arc are worth one point, while baskets from beyond the arc are worth two. Teams have 12 seconds to attempt a shot after gaining possession, making the format significantly faster than the traditional five-a-side game.

item.content:encoded:
”Lomu”, a documentary that tells the life story of the late rugby legend Jonah Lomu will be screened publicly for the first time in Nuku’alofa at Teufaiva Stadium on Wednesday, 29 July.

The documentary was directed by award-winning Tongan-New Zealand filmmaker Vea Mafile’o, with co-director Gavin Fitzgerald, who is based in Ireland. Vea wants to celebrate the life of the rugby legend through the documentary.

Vea’s father comes from Tongoleleka, Ha’apai, and is a rugby man who used to coach rugby at Toloa. Her co-director, Gavin, also loves rugby and grew up adoring Jonah.

“Everyone in overseas, especially in England, loves Jonah. He is really quite popular. Obviously, nowadays, not as popular as before, but the majority of people over there definitely already know him. So it was an exciting project in terms of working with a production company from England and a production company from New Zealand and us coming together to create the story,” she said.

Vea said they interviewed Lomu’s family and close friends, as well as coaches from the rugby world.

“It was very important for us to involve his family, especially his mother and his brother, John.”

“What was really enlightening for me was the understanding that he was this man in the center and then there’s lots of different moving parts; family, rugby, the world, that complicated his life. But he was actually just a very kind hearted — normal Tongan boy.”

She said the role of the media and the people around him put things out there that were not very fair.

“It was important for me to try and unpick some of those narratives that had already been put out there and just to give us that opportunity to celebrate him, because this is the missing piece. We’ve never had the chance to celebrate him as the son of Tonga, and as a son of New Zealand as well, because it’s always been negative.”

Parts of the documentary were filmed in New Zealand, while other scenes were filmed in Tonga at Anahulu.

Vea said it was important to bring more Tongan culture into the documentary and create a narrative that is not the norm for a sports documentary.

Actor, songwriter and artist, JP Foliaki said, “We want people here to see it because we feel that they deserve to see it first.”

Lomu has only been screened at an Australian film festival and a few other film festivals, but this will be the first time it will be shown to the public.

“So that’s going to be essentially making history,” he said,

The public is invited to attend the free documentary screening at Teufaiva Stadium at 5:00 pm on Wednesday, 29 July.

Jonah Lomu died at the age of 40 in New Zealand, 11 years ago this November.

The 1.96-metre (6ft 5in) Jonah made his Test debut in 1994 against France in Christchurch. He earned 63 caps for the All Blacks.

As a global superstar of rugby union, he had a huge impact on the game. He was inducted into the International Rugby Hall of Fame on 9 October 2007 and the IRB Hall of Fame on 24 October 2011.

Lomu was appointed a Member of the New Zealand Order of Merit in the Queen’s Birthday Honours list on 4 June 2007.

His parents emigrated from Tonga to New Zealand, where Jonah was born on 12 May 1975. He attended Wesley College in Auckland.

item.title: Aid to the Pacific region is increasingly debt-driven
item.description: Official Development Finance to the Pacific increased in 2024 reaching US $4.1 billion, ending three years of decline, but a new report says the rise came predominantly from concessional loans, which offset falling year-on-year grants. item.content:encoded:
Official Development Finance to the Pacific increased in 2024 reaching US $4.1 billion, ending three years of decline, but a new report says the rise came predominantly from concessional loans, which offset falling year-on-year grants.

The Pacific aid landscape has stabilised but is increasingly debt-driven, says the Lowy Institute in a new report published today.

The ’Pacific Aid Map 2026’ which tracks aid and development finance flows across the Pacific, notes that Australia remains the largest Pacific Aid partner.

Riley Duke, researcher at the Lowy Institute, said the 2026 version of the interactive map https://pacificaidmap.lowyinstitute.org/ was published today.

“This year we added a currency change tool, so all the data can be viewed in different Pacific currencies, including Tongan paʻanga.”

Australia largest Pacific aid partner Aid to the Pacific is increasingly concentrated among a few major partners, with Australia by far the largest. The United States has cemented a long-term but narrow commitment to the three Compact states.

Australia and multilateral development banks dominate lending to the region. • Australia has signed US $2.4 billion in new loan agreements since 2021. • Strategic infrastructure – ports, airports, telecommunications, and power generation – has accounted for more than half of all new infrastructure commitments since 2020, and infrastructure overall has risen from 15% of regional development finance in 2008 to more than a third by 2019.

The Lowy Institute reported that China maintains aid strategy shift from large-scale lending to high-frequency, small-scale grants. China's Pacific aid remains below its 2010s peak but has stabilised around a high-visibility grant model tied to diplomatic objectives. Loans from its mid-2010s lending boom are now entering acute repayment phases.

” Chinese state-owned firms dominate Pacific infrastructure contracts. Chinese state-owned enterprises have become the dominant construction contractors for Pacific infrastructure, including on projects financed by multilateral development banks. This position has held even as Beijing's own direct financing has declined.

“Chinese SOE s have been involved in more than US $5.1 billion of Pacific infrastructure since 2008, around US $3 billion financed directly by China and the rest by the ADB and World Bank, accounting for roughly 40% of Pacific infrastructure projects by value.”

The Lowy Institute said that the Iran war is the latest in a series of shocks to hit the region, but the scale of the international response is uncertain. Pacific economies have limited capacity to absorb shocks such as the Iran war, leaving them at risk of a "lost decade" of development on top of earlier crises.

Energy insecurity persists despite renewables focus. Pacific Island economies are among the world's most energy insecure. Recent fuel-market volatility has underscored continued dependence on imported fossil fuels despite sustained investment in renewables.

The Lowy Institute is an independent, nonpartisan international policy think tank. The Institute provides high-quality research and distinctive perspectives on the issues and trends shaping Australia’s role in the world. The Pacific Aid Map is now in its ninth year, covering 50,000+ projects and $60 billion in finance since 2008, and it's the most detailed picture available of who's funding what in the region.
